newsitem.title: FRANCE: Thomson-CSF for sale in private placement.
newsitem.headline: Thomson-CSF for sale in private placement.

text.p: The French government relaunched the sale on Wednesday of defence electronics firm Thomson-CSF through a private placement with the aim of creating an internationally competitive defence group.
It said it sought to put together a financially solid group around Thomson-CSF armed with the best technology to take part in the restructuring of the European defence industry.
"It is open to the participation of French and European industrial players in the construction, in stages, around Thomson-CSF," the defence, finance and industry ministries said in a joint statement.

The government's announcement appeared aimed at avoiding the pitfalls that led to the collapse in December of a previous deal to sell the Thomson group, which owns 58 percent of Thomson-CSF and all of television maker Thomson Multimedia (TMM).
Under the new plan, the private placement will hinge on conditions which will be submitted soon to the independent Privatisation Commission, the government said.
The government's original plan to sell Thomson to the Lagardere missiles-to-publishing conglomerate came apart in December after the commission objected to the terms.

Lagardere is expected to renew its bid in competition with its original rival, engineering giant Alcatel Alsthom, which has lined up powerful allies, state-owned Aerospatiale and Dassault Aviation, to boost its chances.

"The Alcatel bid with Aerospatiale and Dassault gives you the same industrial logic (as Lagardere's original proposal), and is a totally French solution," said analyst Charles Armitage at Lehman Brothers.
Lagardere had proposed to merge its missiles business, 50 percent held by British Aerospace, with Thomson-CSF. Lagardere also has a British partner in its Matra Marconi satellite business, GEC Plc.

Armitage said Alcatel's prospects looked stronger the second time around, but he said it was difficult to predict the outcome. "They (the government) may want to say their original decision was right and save face," he said.

And from an industrial point of view, an eventual link-up of Thomson's activities with those of GEC-Marconi would not only generate the biggest cost savings but also create a group with $11 billion in sales capable of rivalling such U.S. giants as Lockheed Martin and Raytheon.
The French statement welcoming interest from European groups appeared to leave the door open for Lagardere and its partners.

Another British-based analyst said it appeared that the government wanted to bring the French defence players into the first stage of the privatisation and then reach out to other European groups, probably through joint venture agreements.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe was reported by a French newspaper to have met the chairmen of Lagardere and Alcatel last week and sought their involvement.

"What they are trying to do is get both Alcatel and Matra (Lagardere) aboard," said Peter Lewis of Jane's Defence Weekly. "But that is going to be very difficult with all the bitterness between the two groups."
"If it (Lagardere) wants to come in alongside Alcatel, the government will be only too happy," said Lewis. "Otherwise they will give it to Alcatel-Aerospatiale-Dassault."
Thomson-CSF welcomed the government's announcement and said its concerns had been assuaged although the management had lobbied for a public share offering to strengthen its position.
A spokesman said Thomson-CSF hoped the privatisation would take place as soon as possible. The French evening newspaper Le Monde said the government aimed to name a buyer before June.
Thomson-CSF shares rallied to a year high on the announcement and were up 4.27 percent at 183 francs at 1320 GMT.
"The privatisation will go ahead through a private placement, quickly, and, no doubt, at a better price than through a public offering," a fund manager said.
Alcatel said the government's decision to sell Thomson-CSF through a private placement "goes in the right direction". A spokesman said the company was waiting to hear the terms.
Officials at Lagardere were not available for comment.
France's decision to call off the sale last year triggered a diplomatic row with South Korea, whose Daewoo Electronics had planned to buy Thomson Multimedia from Lagardere.
The Privatisation Commission had objected to the terms of the sale of hugely indebted TMM to Daewoo for one franc.
A week after suspending the sale, the French government said it would would sell Thomson-CSF stake and TMM separately and recapitalise the latter.
